title: From Sample to Population — The Logic of Inference

info.text: Statistical inference is how a sample earns the right to speak for a population: one law of sample behavior underwrites both ways of going on record — an interval that bets on the truth and a test that puts a claim on trial, with named margins and named mistakes.

clusters.name: Two worlds
clusters.fact: There is the population you care about and the sample you can actually afford — and each side has its own number for the same question: the parameter and the statistic.

parameter.text: A number describing the population — the true share, the true mean μ. Almost never observable; always the target.

population.text: Everyone (or everything) the question is really about — every voter, every widget. What you'd measure if measuring everything were possible.

sample.text: The part of the population actually observed; the 1,200 people polled. Inference's only source of evidence.

statistic.text: A number computed from the sample — the poll's 53%, the sample mean x̄. The observable stand-in for its parameter.

clusters.name: The law of sample behavior
clusters.fact: Samples refuse to agree with each other — but their disagreement has a shape, a width, and a guarantee, and that law is what lets one noisy sample speak for everyone.

central limit theorem.text: For large samples, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal — centered on the parameter — whatever shape the population itself has.

sampling distribution.text: The collection of a statistic's values over every possible sample — the pattern repeated polls trace. Where a statistic's behavior lives.

standard error.text: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution — the typical distance a statistic lands from the parameter. It shrinks as samples grow: SE = σ/√n.

clusters.name: Estimation
clusters.fact: The honest way to answer 'what is the parameter?' is a guess plus its price: one number from the sample, an interval around it, a stated hit rate, and the margin that sets the interval's width.

confidence interval.text: The point estimate plus and minus a margin of error — an interval the method catches the parameter in, sample after sample, at the promised rate.

confidence level.text: The promised hit rate: 95% of intervals built this way contain the true parameter. A property of the method, not of any one interval.

margin of error.text: The half-width of the interval: a critical value times the standard error. The price of the guess, paid in sampling variability.

point estimate.text: The single number a sample offers for the parameter — the statistic itself, taken as the best guess.

clusters.name: Testing a claim
clusters.fact: Put a default claim on trial, agree in advance on what counts as evidence against it, and let the sample testify — the machinery that turns a surprising statistic into a decision.

alternative hypothesis.text: The claim the evidence supports if the null is rejected — the researcher's suspicion, stated before the data arrives.

null hypothesis.text: The default claim on trial — no effect, no difference, exactly 50%. It is never proven; the only decisive verdict is rejection.

p-value.text: Assuming the null is true, the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one. Small means the sample is hard to explain by luck.

significance level.text: The pre-declared threshold α for surprise — commonly 0.05. A p-value below it rejects the null; α is also the type I error rate accepted by decree.

clusters.name: The two mistakes
clusters.fact: A verdict can miss in exactly two directions — convicting the innocent or freeing the guilty — and statistics names both mistakes and the prize for avoiding the second one.

power.text: The chance the test catches a real effect: 1 − β. It grows with sample size, clearer effects, and a more generous α.

type I error.text: Rejecting a null that was actually true — the false alarm. Its long-run rate is the significance level α.

links.href: wiki:Type I and type II errors

type II error.text: Failing to reject a null that was actually false — the missed discovery. Its probability is β.

links.href: wiki:Type I and type II errors
wiki:Type I and type II errors

bridges.fact: Inference is the whole move: the parameter cannot be seen, so the sample's statistic speaks for it — estimation turns a statistic into an interval bet, and testing puts a claim about the parameter on trial before the statistic.

Each sample yields its own statistic, but the statistic's sampling distribution is centered on the parameter itself — the mean of all the sample means is μ. That centering is where the sample world touches the population world.

A confidence interval is the point estimate plus and minus a critical value times the standard error: the margin of error is sampling variability priced at the chosen confidence — which is why bigger samples buy narrower intervals.

The p-value locates this sample's statistic inside the sampling distribution the null hypothesis predicts: the question is how far into the tail a statistic must fall before the null stops being believable.

Every test ends in one of two verdicts — reject the null or keep it — and each can be wrong in exactly one way: type I fires at a true claim, type II misses a false one. The significance level is the type I rate set by decree; power is one minus the type II rate.

links.href: wiki:Type I and type II errors

lenses.prompt: A poll contacts 1,200 voters and reports 53% support. Which two terms name, respectively, everyone the conclusion is about and the 1,200 actually contacted?
lenses.explanation: Every voter in the country is the population — the whole the conclusion is about. The 1,200 actually polled are the sample, inference's only source of evidence.

reasons.population: all voters — the whole the poll exists to speak about
reasons.sample: the 1,200 actually contacted — the observed part

lenses.prompt: The true share of all voters who support the measure is one number nobody can see; the poll's 53% is its computed stand-in. Which two terms name them?
lenses.explanation: The true support among all voters is the parameter — a number nobody can observe. The poll's 53% is a statistic, computed from the sample, standing in for it.

lenses.prompt: Pollsters repeat the poll many times, and each poll lands on a slightly different percentage. Which term names the pattern those repeated results trace?
lenses.explanation: Repeat the poll with new samples and each gets its own percentage; the pattern those values trace is the sampling distribution. The standard error measures its width rather than being the pattern, and the central limit theorem supplies its shape.

reasons.sampling distribution: the collection of a statistic's values over all possible samples

lenses.prompt: The report reads '53%, ±3 points.' Which two terms name the ±3 points and the interval they build around 53%?
lenses.explanation: The ±3 points are the margin of error — the interval's half-width; the interval it builds around 53% is the confidence interval. The point estimate is the 53% itself, not the ±3, and the confidence level is the promise, not the width.

reasons.confidence interval: 53% minus 3 to 53% plus 3 — the interval the method stands behind
reasons.margin of error: the ±3 — a critical value times the standard error

lenses.prompt: A skeptic assumes the measure truly has exactly 50% support and asks how unlikely a 53% poll would be. Which two terms name the default assumption and the probability of a result at least that surprising under it?
lenses.explanation: The skeptic's working assumption — exactly 50%, nothing special — is the null hypothesis. The probability of a result at least this surprising under that assumption is the p-value. The alternative is the claim waiting if the null loses, and the significance level is the threshold, not the computed probability.

reasons.null hypothesis: the default on trial: no effect, exactly 50%
reasons.p-value: the probability, under the null, of a result at least this extreme

lenses.prompt: The test rejects the 50% claim — but suppose the truth really was 50%. Which term names the mistake just made, and which names the long-run chance of making it that was set in advance?
lenses.explanation: Rejecting a null that was actually true is a type I error — the false alarm — and the test's long-run chance of committing it is exactly the significance level α set in advance. The type II error is the opposite miss, and power is its complement.

reasons.significance level: α — the type I rate accepted by decree before the data arrived
reasons.type I error: rejecting a true null — the false alarm

learningIntroduction.summary: How a sample earns the right to speak for a population: the law of sample behavior underwrites an interval bet on the truth and a trial verdict on a claim, with named margins and named mistakes.

content.text:
A poll of 1,200 voters says 53%. Nobody polled everyone — so how can the number mean anything? Statistical inference is the answer, and this lesson walks its machinery: the two worlds every number lives in, the law that lets one world speak for the other, and the two ways to put a sample on record — an interval bet and a trial verdict.

## Two worlds, two numbers

The population is everyone — or everything — the question is about; the sample is the part actually observed. Each world has its own number for the same question: the parameter is the population's value, the true share or true mean, and the statistic is the sample's computation of it. The parameter is almost never observable; the statistic is all we ever hold. Everything in this lesson is traffic between those two kinds of number.

## The law of sample behavior

Draw a different 1,200 people and the statistic moves — that is sampling variability, and it is not chaos. Imagine every possible sample's statistic laid out: that collection is the sampling distribution, and it has a measurable width called the standard error, which shrinks as samples grow. Its shape is the punchline: the central limit theorem says that for large samples the distribution of sample means is approximately normal — bell-shaped and centered exactly on the parameter — no matter what the population itself looks like. One noisy sample can speak for everyone because the crowd of all possible samples behaves predictably.

## Estimation: betting an interval

To answer 'what is the parameter?', start with the point estimate — the statistic itself, the single best guess. An honest report never stops there: a confidence interval adds and subtracts a margin of error, and the margin is the standard error priced by how sure you demand to be. The confidence level is that promise read across repeated use: intervals built this way catch the true parameter in 95% of samples — not that this particular interval is 95% likely to be right, but that the method hits 95% of the time.

## Testing a claim

Sometimes the question is not 'what is it?' but 'could this claim be true?'. Hypothesis testing puts a default — the null hypothesis, the claim of no effect, no difference, exactly 50% — on trial, with the alternative hypothesis waiting in case the evidence overturns it. The p-value is the evidence meter: assuming the null is true, it is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. The significance level, chosen before the data arrives, is the threshold — how surprising a sample must be before the default loses and is rejected.

## The two mistakes

Any verdict can miss in two directions. A type I error rejects a null that was actually true — the false alarm. A type II error keeps a null that was actually false — the missed discovery. The significance level is the type I rate accepted by decree, and the mistakes pull against each other: make rejection harder and false alarms fall while missed discoveries rise. The prize for escaping the second mistake has a name — power, the chance a test catches an effect that is really there, which grows with bigger samples and clearer effects.

The poll's '53%, ±3 points' is now a whole sentence: a statistic estimating a parameter, a margin of error priced by the standard error, a method that hits 95% of the time — and, if you ran a formal test against 50%, a verdict whose error rates were chosen in advance.
